translations.text: Truly, every man needs to look after his soul's journey himself, and to think how grave it will be when death comes and sunders the kinship of those who were together before, body and soul!
It will be long afterwards that the spirit receives from God himself either punishment or glory, just as that earthen vessel earlier earned for it in the world.

The spirit must come, crying out in its sorrows, always after seven nights, to find the body that it had long worn before, for three hundred years, unless the eternal Lord, almighty God, brings about the end of the world before then.

Then, full of care, it calls in a cold voice; the spirit speaks grimly to the dust: "Listen, you dry and dreary thing, why did you torment me? You filth of the earth, wholly withering away, image of clay!
You gave little thought to what would become of your soul's journey afterwards, once it had been led out of the body!

Lo, you tormented me, accursed one! Indeed, you food for worms, little did you think how long it would be until now, and that the Lord almighty sent a soul into you from above, from the heavens, through an angel, by his own hand,
the almighty Creator, from his majesty, and then redeemed you with the holy blood; and you bound me with harsh hunger and held me captive in the torments of hell!
I dwelt within you. I could not get out of you, enclosed in flesh, and your sinful lusts pressed in on me.
Very often it seemed to me that it would be thirty thousand years until your death-day. Listen, I waited for our parting in hardship. Now the end is not too good!
You were proud with feasting and sated with wine, and you swaggered in your glory, while I thirsted for God's body, the spirit's drink.
If you had then considered here in life, while I had to dwell in you in the world, that you were strongly driven by the flesh and by sinful lusts, and yet were established through me,
and that I was a spirit in you sent from God, you would never have prepared such hard torments of hell for me through the lust of your needs.
Yet now you must suffer the shame of my disgraces on the great day, when the Only-begotten gathers all mankind together.

Now you are no dearer to anyone living, to any person as a companion, neither to mother nor father nor any kinsman, than the black raven is, since I alone journeyed out of you by the hand of the very one by whom I had earlier been sent in.

Now the red ornaments cannot take you away from here, nor gold, nor silver, nor any of your goods. Instead the bones must stay here, stripped bare and torn from the sinews, and your soul must often seek you out against my will and reproach you with words, as you did to me.
You are dumb and deaf, and your joys are nothing at all.

Yet I must seek you out by night because I have to, pained by sins, and soon turn away from you again at cockcrow, when holy men sing songs of praise to the living God, to seek the homes that you assigned to me before,

and the merciless dwelling place. And many earthworms shall chew you, dark creatures, greedy and ravenous, shall tear you from the sinews. Your boasts, which you displayed to men here on earth, are nothing.
Therefore it would have been much better for you than if all the riches of the earth were yours (unless you shared them with the Lord himself)
if at the creation you had become a bird, or a fish in the sea, or a beast of the earth seeking its food, a field-roaming animal without wisdom, or the fiercest of the wild beasts in the wilderness,
if God had so willed, yes, even if you were the worst of the race of serpents, rather than ever becoming a man on earth or ever having to receive baptism.
Then you must answer for both of us on the great day, when the wounds that sinful men once inflicted in the world will be revealed to all men.
Then the Lord himself will hear of the deeds and will hear from every man, by the speech of his mouth, the repayment for the wounds. But what will you say to the Lord there on Doomsday?
Then there will be no joint grown on a limb so small that you will not have to pay what is due for each one separately, when the Lord is stern at the judgement.
But what shall we two do when he has given us birth a second time?
Then we must together afterwards partake of such miseries as you assigned to us before."
So it reviles that hoard of flesh. Then it must go on its way, troubled by its deeds, and seek the abyss of hell, not the joys of heaven.
The dust lies where it was. It cannot give it any answer, nor promise the sad spirit any refuge there, help or comfort.

The head is split apart, the hands pulled from their joints, the jaws gape, the palate is torn apart, the sinews are sucked away, the neck is chewed through. Fierce worms plunder the ribs and drink the corpse in swarms, thirsty for gore.
The tongue is torn into ten pieces as a comfort to the hungry ones. Therefore it cannot nimbly exchange words with the accursed spirit.
Glutton is the name of the worm whose jaws are sharper than a needle. He is the first of all to venture into the earth-pit. He tears the tongue apart and bores through the teeth, [?]

[?] and opens the way to the carrion-feast for others, and eats through the eyes from above into the head as a feast for worms, when the accursed body that he long before clothed with garments has grown cold.
Then it is food for worms, a meal in the earth. That can be a reminder to every man of wise mind.
